opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that made Genie 2 really exciting for us was that it felt like a genuine step change rather than just an incremental improvement. With the original Genie, we were working in this 2D platformer setting, and it was a really nice proof of concept: you could learn an action-controllable world model purely from videos, without any action labels, and then generate new environments from a single image prompt. But it was fairly constrained. The worlds were 2D, the resolution was low, and the consistency only held for a short horizon.

With Genie 2, the question was basically: does this idea scale? Can you go from these toy-ish 2D worlds to rich, diverse 3D environments? And what we found was that a lot of really interesting capabilities started to emerge once we trained at larger scale on a broad distribution of 3D video data. The model could handle things like object interactions, character animation, physics like water or smoke, lighting and reflections, and, importantly, some degree of long-horizon memory. So if you looked away from part of the world and then looked back, it would often remember what was there and render it consistently. None of that was explicitly programmed in; it came out of the scale and the data.

From a research perspective, the reason I care about that so much is the bigger motivation behind the whole project, which is around training generally capable embodied agents. One of the major bottlenecks in that space has always been the availability of rich, diverse training environments. Historically we've relied on hand-designed simulators or games, and those are expensive to build and there's only so many of them. If you can instead generate an essentially unlimited variety of interactive 3D worlds from a prompt, whether an image or a text description, then you potentially unlock a path toward much more general agents, because you can keep generating new and challenging environments for them to learn in. That's the open-endedness angle I've been interested in for a long time.

So, for me, Genie 2 was exciting because it suggested that foundation world models might actually be a viable route to that. It's obviously not perfect. There are still issues with consistency over very long horizons, and with the fidelity of some interactions. But seeing it work at all in 3D, with these emergent properties, made it feel like this direction was real and worth pushing on much harder.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that got me most excited about Genie 2 was really about what it told us about scaling. With the original Genie, we were working with 2D platformer-style worlds, and we trained on this huge corpus of internet videos of people playing games, and the model learned to generate playable worlds where you could actually move a character around with latent actions it had figured out on its own. That was already a surprising result. But the obvious question everyone asked, and we asked ourselves, was whether this would hold up when you move to something much richer and much harder, like 3D.

And Genie 2 was essentially the answer to that question. We scaled up the model and the data, and we found that you could generate these 3D environments from a single prompt image, and you'd get things like object permanence, so if you look away from something and look back, it's still there. You'd get physics-like behavior, water, gravity, lighting, reflections, characters that respond to your inputs. None of that was hand-coded. It emerged from training on video. And for me the exciting part wasn't any single one of those capabilities, it was that the recipe transferred. It suggested world models follow a similar scaling story to what we've seen with language models, where you add compute and data and you get qualitatively new behavior rather than just marginal improvement.

The other reason I found it exciting is what it unlocks for agents. One of the big bottlenecks in training embodied or game-playing agents is the environments themselves. You need diverse, interesting worlds, and historically those are expensive to build by hand. If you can generate an essentially unlimited curriculum of novel 3D worlds, you've suddenly got a path to training agents that generalize, because they're not overfitting to a handful of fixed environments. So Genie 2 felt like a step toward world models as a foundation for agent research, not just as a cool generative demo. That combination, the scaling evidence plus the downstream implications for agents, is what made it feel like a real result rather than just an impressive video.

astra-6.text:
What excited me was that it suggested we could move beyond a small set of environments that we’ve built by hand. With Genie 2, you can start from an image and generate a 3D world that an agent can interact with, where its actions affect what happens next. That gives us a potentially much broader space of environments for training and evaluating agents.

And the interesting part isn’t just generating something that looks convincing. It’s maintaining a coherent world as you move around and interact with it. If we can scale that capability, we can start to challenge agents with unfamiliar situations and ask whether they’ve learned skills that actually generalize. That’s why I saw it as an exciting research step toward more general agents.

sol-6.1.text:
What excited me was the idea that you could generate a world and then actually interact with it. Moving into 3D makes that particularly interesting, because as you move around, the model has to maintain a coherent environment and respond to your actions over time.

And from an agent-learning perspective, that opens up a really compelling possibility: generating a much broader range of environments for agents to learn in. Instead of being limited to the worlds we build by hand, we could start to create new situations and challenges on demand. That connection between generating worlds and training agents is what makes this such an exciting research direction.
